config.prompt: A 100 N weight hangs from two ropes at 60° on either side of vertical. What tension does each rope carry?
config.why: Equilibrium: 2T cos 60° = 100, so T = 100 N. At 45° it is 70.7 N; at 80°, about 288 N — shallow ropes are dangerous.

activities.anchor: Projection is the dot product's geometric act
activities.caption: rebuild least squares as a projection
activities.name: laProjectionOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild least-squares regression as a projection:
items: Stack the observed responses into a vector b
The predictor columns span a subspace of observation space
Project b onto that subspace — the fitted values p
The residual b − p is orthogonal to every predictor column
Solve the normal equations AᵀA x = Aᵀb for the coefficients
config.why: Orthogonality of the residual is the defining property of a projection, and it is exactly what the normal equations encode.

config.prompt: Find the line where the parallelogram proof goes wrong:
lines: Let A, B, C, D have position vectors a, b, c, d.
The midpoint of AC is (a + c)/2; the midpoint of BD is (b + d)/2.
ABCD is a parallelogram, so AB = DC: b − a = c − d.
Rearranging gives a + c = b + d, so the two diagonals share a midpoint.
Therefore the diagonals bisect each other — but only because ABCD is a rectangle.
config.correction: The rectangle is irrelevant: the proof used only AB = DC, which holds for every parallelogram.
config.why: No right angle was ever used; the argument is valid for any parallelogram, rectangle or not.

activities.anchor: Solving systems is the applied payoff
activities.caption: pick the solver for 10,000 equations
activities.name: laSolveBranch

config.root: You must solve a sparse system of 10,000 linear equations in 10,000 unknowns. Choose a route.

start.text: The coefficient matrix is sparse and invertible. What do you reach for?

choices.label: Gaussian elimination with a sparse ordering
choices.feedback: Yes — elimination exploits sparsity and scales; this is what structural and weather solvers do.

choices.label: Compute the inverse matrix, then multiply
choices.feedback: Inverting is far more expensive and fills in zeros; elimination solves directly.

choices.label: Cramer's rule with determinants
choices.feedback: Cramer's rule is exponential in the number of unknowns — fine for 2×2, hopeless here.

elim.text: Direct elimination (with a good ordering) is the workhorse; iterative methods take over when the system is enormous.

inverse.text: Forming A⁻¹ costs more than solving Ax = b once, and it destroys sparsity.

choices.label: So what should be done instead?
choices.feedback: Factorise or eliminate directly — never invert explicitly.

cramer.text: Cramer's rule needs one determinant per unknown: 10,000 determinants of size 10,000.

config.why: Solution method follows structure: sparsity favours elimination; explicit inverses are almost never the right move.

activities.caption: eigen-decomposition versus SVD — drag the divider
activities.name: laSvdCompare

before.label: eigendecomposition
before.text: A = QΛQ⁻¹ needs a square matrix and a full set of eigenvectors; defective matrices refuse.

after.label: SVD
after.text: A = UΣVᵀ works for every matrix, square or rectangular; singular values rank the information.

config.why: SVD trades eigenvectors for two orthonormal bases, which is why it always exists — and why truncating small singular values is the provably best low-rank approximation.

activities.anchor: For a matrix A, an eigenvector satisfies
activities.caption: true or false — reading eigenvalues
activities.name: laEigenJudge

statements.s: An eigenvector is a direction the matrix stretches or shrinks but never rotates.
statements.why: Av = λv: the output lies on the same line as the input.

statements.s: PageRank's ranking vector is the eigenvector of the link matrix with eigenvalue 1.
statements.why: A steady state of the random surfer is exactly a fixed direction of the link matrix.

statements.s: A negative real part of an eigenvalue means disturbances grow without bound.
statements.why: Negative real part means decay toward equilibrium; growth needs a positive real part.

activities.anchor: The axioms of a vector space never mention numbers
activities.caption: pair each object with why it is a vector space
activities.name: laSpanMatch

config.prompt: Pair each object with why it counts as a vector space:

pairs.right: add pointwise and scale; Fourier series writes a signal in a basis of sines
a Hilbert space; measurement is projection onto a basis direction
a million-dimensional vector; PCA finds the important directions

config.why: The axioms never mention arrows or coordinates — anything that adds and scales obeying the rules is a vector space, and the geometry of span, basis and projection carries over.
